turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no reason to be blind to his misfortunes, for I have heard the true account of them from himself.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must confess, your accusation stings, though I do not expect your understanding or sympathy at this moment. I shall not attempt to justify myself on this point, as it is clear my actions have left much to be desired in your eyes.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I cannot pretend to feel what I do not feel, but I can assure you that the least I owe myself is to know what I do feel.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware that my actions have led to this misunderstanding, Miss Bennet. Yet, I cannot help but feel a pang of regret that our conversation has reached this point.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I must be frank. Your manners and your pride have long offended me, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Your first proposal was an insult to my understanding and my feelings.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your candor is commendable, but your words wound me deeply. I confess, I did not expect such vehemence in your rejection.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am well aware that my words must be cutting, but I cannot help it when my feelings are so strong. Your pride has been my constant companion, Mr. Darcy, and I cannot ignore the pain it has caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your insight is clear and your words, though harsh, are just. I must endure the consequences of my actions and the judgments they have brought upon me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: You have brought this upon yourself, Mr. Darcy. Your own actions have led to this moment, and your pride has blinded you to the harm you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your accusations are not unjust, Miss Bennet. I am aware of my shortcomings and the pain I have inflicted. Yet, I cannot help but confess my love for you, despite the obvious obstacles.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am surprised by your confession, Mr. Darcy, but your past actions make it difficult for me to accept such feelings from you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I am well aware of your feelings, Mr. Darcy, but your past behaviour towards my family and friends makes it impossible for me to consider your confession with anything but the utmost disdain.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand your feelings, Miss Bennet, and I do not seek to trivialize them. My past actions have indeed caused you great pain, and for that, I am truly sorry. Yet, my feelings for you remain unchanged.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: My feelings towards you, Mr. Darcy, are clear. Your pride and my prejudice have led us to this point, and it is not one I am ready to overlook.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I comprehend the gravity of your feelings, Elizabeth. It is not within my power to change the past, but I hope that, given time, you may come to see the sincerity of my heart.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Your sincerity, Mr. Darcy, does not change the truth of my feelings. I cannot look past the pain you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I must accept that my past actions have led to this outcome, Elizabeth. I shall endeavour to earn your regard over time, if you will permit me the chance.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I appreciate your sentiment, Mr. Darcy, but I must think on this. There is much to consider and little to ease the hurt you have caused.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I understand the weight of my actions, Elizabeth. I shall respect your need for time and space to consider our relationship.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I must take my leave now, Mr. Darcy. There is much to contemplate and I need time to myself.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
